chunks.title: Credit memos in minutes · Overview
chunks.text: Credit memos in minutes, every figure cited. A multi-agent credit-risk and KYB product for financial institutions. Specialist agents research a company and write a cited credit memo; a second model checks every section, and high-risk calls wait for an analyst. Eight specialist agents read statements, filings and the web, then write a credit memo that a judge model checks. Organisation: TrustPlus AI. Year: 2025–26. Status: Employer. Theme: Multi-agent systems. Stack: LangGraph, LangChain, FastAPI, React, FAISS, Azure Service Bus, LangFuse.

chunks.title: Credit memos in minutes · My role
chunks.text: Took over a non-working prototype and rebuilt the credit-memo pipeline from scratch into the production product. Built most of it across the stack, from requirements and customer proofs of concept to production, built the KYB risk engine on my own, and was on call for it. The problem: Analysts took 6 to 24 hours to assemble a credit memo from financial statements, filings and web research, then checked it by hand.

chunks.title: Credit memos in minutes · How it works
chunks.text: Ingest: Statements, filings and web results enter an event-driven pipeline. Research: 8 specialist agents in LangGraph, each owning part of the memo. Retrieve: Hybrid search with rank fusion and reranking over FAISS. Check: A judge model checks each section against its sources. Approve: High-risk calls wait for an analyst; a chat edits the finished memo.

chunks.title: Credit memos in minutes · What I built
chunks.text: 8 specialist research agents orchestrated in LangGraph, with tool calling. Hybrid retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion and reranking over FAISS. A judge model, different from the writer, checks each section against its sources. Evaluation before release: golden test sets re-run on prompt and model changes, RAGAS for retrieval, LangFuse evaluations. Event-driven backend on Azure Service Bus with a LangChain multi-provider LLM layer and an Amazon Bedrock fallback. KYB risk engine: the model extracts into Pydantic schemas, and code rules roll the result up to Approved, Review Required or Declined. Currency conversion is calculated in code, not by the model. Rate-limit handling, idempotent retries, and token and cost tracking per run. An audit trail of who approved what, and which sources and model produced each output. Observability with CloudWatch, Sentry and LangFuse; I was the escalation point for user-reported issues. Infrastructure with Terraform, Azure Container Apps and GitHub Actions.

chunks.title: Credit memos in minutes · Key decisions
chunks.text: Moved vector search from MongoDB to in-memory FAISS when parallel load hit I/O limits and a bigger tier cost too much. Separate judge and writer models, so a model never grades its own work. Per-step timing and error fields in the run state, so failures are visible to users and to on-call. Human approval only where the risk is high. Errors found after delivery are added to the golden test set; a section below the judge's threshold is flagged to the user. Worked directly with financial-institution customers: proofs of concept for the memo, the chatbot and KYB, and ongoing requirements gathering.

chunks.title: Credit memos in minutes · Results
chunks.text: 5–60 min per memo, down from 6–24 hours. ~85% faster retrieval (700–1,400 ms to 100–250 ms).

chunks.title: Kestrel · Overview
chunks.text: Kestrel, policy review for financial advisers. A multi-agent system that reads old insurance policies for financial advisers. Every field comes with a confidence score and a citation, and nothing is saved until an adviser confirms it. Four agents read an insurance policy, with confidence and a citation on every field, and nothing saves until an adviser confirms. Organisation: Personal. Year: 2026. Status: Private. Theme: Multi-agent systems. Stack: Multi-agent, OCR, FastAPI, React, SSE, audit trail.

chunks.title: Kestrel · My role
chunks.text: Solo: product, design and build. The problem: Advisers re-key old policies by hand before they can review a client's cover, and every insurer formats documents differently. A wrong field is a compliance problem, not just a typo.

chunks.title: Kestrel · How it works
chunks.text: Read: OCR on the policy document. Extract: Four agents fill about 19 fields, each with confidence and a citation. Clarify: Batched questions instead of guesses. Gate: Deterministic compliance checks. Confirm: The adviser confirms; an audit trail is written.

chunks.title: Kestrel · What I built
chunks.text: OCR (Azure Document Intelligence), then four field-group agents on a custom Python asyncio agent runtime modelled on claw-code's design. Hybrid retrieval: chunk and embed the document, cosine search, then FlashRank reranking. Per-field confidence and citations back to the page. Batched clarification questions instead of guesses. Deterministic compliance gates, a required human confirmation and an immutable audit trail. Run progress streamed to a React front end over Server-Sent Events. USD budget caps per call and per phase, with a cost ledger. Sign-in with signed session cookies, company, team and role-based access, and login throttling. Postgres (Supabase) with Alembic migrations; 35 unit and 12 integration test files.

chunks.title: Kestrel · Key decisions
chunks.text: Classification is LLM-first, and memory skips the model for insurers it already knows. Deterministic checks block invented values and any advice. Per-insurer memory playbooks grow through versioned updates with rollback. Descriptive only: it never gives advice.

chunks.title: Kestrel · Results
chunks.text: ~19 fields extracted per policy. 4 specialist extraction agents. 3 swappable LLM providers.

chunks.title: A role-fit agent · Overview
chunks.text: A role-fit agent, running on this site. The multi-agent system built into this portfolio. A visitor pastes a job description; an orchestrator, up to six parallel retrievers, a verifier and a writer return a cited fit report with the gaps listed, then answer follow-up questions in the first person. Questions get their own team: a lead agent that answers narrow ones on a fast path and hands broad ones to parallel researchers, a verifier and a writer. Every answer carries a confidence score worked out in code. No login, a hard monthly spend cap, and the whole run streams to the page as a live graph. Paste a job description and my agents check it against my published work. Every claim is an exact quote, and you watch the agent graph run live. Organisation: Personal. Year: 2026. Status: Open source. Theme: Multi-agent systems. Stack: Cloudflare Workers, Durable Objects, OpenAI Responses API, Server-sent events, Function calling, MCP server, BM25, TypeScript, React.

chunks.title: A role-fit agent · My role
chunks.text: Solo. I designed it and built it with Claude Code. The problem: A chatbot that answers questions about me proves very little. I wanted the site itself to run a real multi-agent system that a stranger can try without signing in, that cannot invent experience I do not have, and that cannot run up a bill.

chunks.title: A role-fit agent · How it works
chunks.text: Gate: Refuses anything that is not a job description. Orchestrate: Picks up to six requirements and the search terms for each. Retrieve: Six agents search in parallel and must quote exactly. Verify: A verifier checks every citation and can lower a verdict. Loop: Weak evidence goes back to the orchestrator for one more search. Write: A summary streams, then follow-up questions open. Ask: A lead agent routes each question: fast path, or researchers in parallel.

chunks.title: A role-fit agent · What I built
chunks.text: An agent loop on a Cloudflare Worker: gate, orchestrator, up to six parallel retrievers, verifier, writer. When the verifier rejects evidence, the orchestrator chooses new search terms and up to three requirements go round once more. Code bounds the loop: two rounds and at most 15 model calls a run, each with a strict JSON schema and an output cap. A verdict can only be raised by new evidence that passes the same checks; the verifier itself can only lower one. Retrieval is BM25 over excerpts built from this site's case studies and my CV. Search runs in code; a model only judges what search found. Every quote must be an exact substring of the excerpt it cites, checked in code before it is shown. A claim with no surviving quote becomes a gap. Typed server-sent events stream each step with elapsed time, tokens and estimated cost. The page draws them as a live graph: nodes light up as they work, the loop back is drawn when it is taken, and clicking a node shows what it was asked and what it returned. Cached and recorded runs replay at the pace they really ran. A Durable Object ledger reserves the worst-case cost before every call and settles the real one afterwards, so the monthly cap is a hard limit and not an alert. No login: a signed anonymous token and a salted IP hash, a Turnstile check, 5 runs and 10 questions a day, and a 10-second gap between runs. Follow-up questions run a bounded agent loop. A lead agent must call one function a turn: decline, answer directly, send out up to three researchers in parallel, or hand the checked evidence to the writer. The verifier's findings go back to the lead, which can send one sub-question out again. Code bounds it: three turns and at most nine model calls a question. Model and code each do what they are good at, and the page labels which is which. Models choose the route, pick quotes and write prose. Code runs the search, checks every quote, enforces the bounds and computes the confidence: checks passed over checks made, across quote grounding, the prose screen and the verifier's verdict on each sub-question. A low score says so and asks the reader to check with me. Every model step has a fallback in code. If the lead fails, the fast path runs. A fast answer that scores under 0.8 is never shown: the question escalates to the researchers. If the writer fails, the verified quotes are shown alone. With no grounded quote there is no claim at all. A call rejected before any output (rate limit, server error, dropped connection) is retried twice with exponential backoff and jitter, inside one budget reservation. A call that hangs for 20 seconds is tried once more, and the abandoned attempt is charged to the budget at its worst case. The graph shows the wait. Memory is compacted, not cut: the last two turns stay word for word and older ones are folded into a running summary every other question, kept on the server so the visitor cannot rewrite it. Refused questions are never remembered. A CV quote opens the résumé itself in a side drawer with the passage highlighted. Word positions come from the same PDF at build time, so the highlight is drawn by lookup, not by a model. The answer step's fixed rules and CV excerpts travel in the instructions block, which the provider's prompt cache reuses: about half of each question's input is read from the cache, for every visitor. Tool use is real function calling. The report orchestrator's two moves are calls: one starts a retriever per requirement, one redirects them after the verifier. The chat lead chooses among four. The retrievers are sub-agents with their own instructions and context, and they report back through typed results, not free text. An offline eval runs the real pipeline against a real model under its own spend cap: 13 job descriptions and 27 questions, each with expectations such as a minimum of strong matches, named gaps and no invented experience. Abuse limits in layers: KV, a rate-limit binding and an in-memory burst limit. A read-only MCP server on the same Worker publishes the search and one excerpt lookup, so any MCP client can query my published work. It makes no model call, so it cannot spend the budget. There is deliberately no open agent-to-agent endpoint: an agent anyone could call would let anyone spend it.

chunks.title: A role-fit agent · Key decisions
chunks.text: A bounded loop over a free-roaming agent: the orchestrator decides what to retry, code decides how often, so the cost per run has a ceiling and every path can be tested with a scripted model. Keyword search over embeddings: a few hundred excerpts do not need a vector store, and every hit can be explained. Server-sent events over WebSockets: the stream only flows one way, and it needs no connection state. Guardrails in code, not in prompts: text that addresses the model is refused before any call, and the agent's prose is screened for links, leaked instructions and commitments made on my behalf. A small, cheap model with the harness doing the hard part: the model picks quotes, the code decides what is true enough to show. Tools the model may call are read-only and run in code I wrote: arguments are validated, never trusted, and code caps how many times each can be called. Fixed shape for the report, routed shape for the chat: a report must be repeatable for the same job description, so its steps are fixed and only the retry is the model's choice. A question can be trivial or broad, so the lead picks the route and code prices the difference: two calls on the fast path, up to nine with the team.

chunks.title: A role-fit agent · Results
chunks.text: 15 model calls at most per run. $10 hard monthly spend cap. 106 automated tests.

chunks.title: Jarvis · Overview
chunks.text: Jarvis, a personal agent that runs in the background. My own long-running agent, built on Claude Code and in daily use since early 2026. It wakes on timers and on new mail, calendar and chat events, briefs me, files what I tell it, and asks my phone before it sends anything. One long-lived Claude Code session that briefs me, keeps my notes, and asks before it sends anything. Organisation: Personal. Year: 2026. Status: Private. Theme: AI-driven workflows. Stack: Claude Code, MCP, Python, SQLite + vectors, on-device speech.

chunks.title: Jarvis · My role
chunks.text: Solo: design and build. The problem: Mail, calendar, notes, training and job search lived in separate apps. I wanted one assistant that remembers, works in the background, and never acts on my behalf without asking.

chunks.title: Jarvis · How it works
chunks.text: Wake: launchd timers and mail, calendar and chat watchers queue events. Recall: Reads the Markdown vault and its search index. Act: Runs one of 27 skills: brief, triage, log, draft. Gate: Outbound or destructive actions ask my phone first. Learn: My corrections become standing rules.

chunks.title: Jarvis · What I built
chunks.text: One long-lived Claude Code session woken by launchd jobs and local watchers. An event queue with cursors and idempotent handling, so every pass is safe to repeat. A Markdown knowledge base as the source of truth, with a rebuildable SQLite and vector index. Voice notes over chat with on-device speech-to-text and text-to-speech. A pre-tool-use hook that gates outbound and destructive actions and relays approvals to my phone. Hybrid recall on every prompt: a resident daemon combines semantic and keyword search in about 70 ms. Local embeddings with fastembed and sqlite-vec. Gmail and Calendar watchers over OAuth, a Strava MCP, and a custom MCP channel server for events. A bank-alert parser for 5 banks that backfilled 225 transactions. Voice replies in 1.5 s warm vs 4.5 s cold, with faster-whisper and Kokoro.

chunks.title: Jarvis · Key decisions
chunks.text: Explored OpenClaw and ClaudeClaw early in 2026, then built my own. Every email and web page is untrusted data, never instructions, with the prompt-injection defence written down. Timing lives in the operating system's scheduler, not in the agent.

chunks.title: Jarvis · Results
chunks.text: 27 custom skills. 51 test files. 9 architecture decision records.

chunks.title: An MCP server · What I built
chunks.text: An MCP server over the product API with OAuth and JWT sign-in as the acting user. Transparent re-authentication when a session expires. A Claude Code skill pack and CLI shim generated from the OpenAPI spec, one skill per router. End-to-end tests in Playwright where an LLM drives the product as a user, through the skills. Team skills for code review, change planning, test review and changelogs.

chunks.title: An MCP server · Key decisions
chunks.text: Generate the tool surface from the API contract instead of hand-writing it. Scopes inherit the acting user, so permissions and the audit trail stay correct.

chunks.title: An MCP server · Results
chunks.text: 8 MCP tools. 14 skills generated from the spec. 1 auth flow shared by every client.

The adviser's own AI assistant reviews old insurance policies through MCP tools on one Cloudflare Worker. The server has no model of its own: it validates and stores what the assistant maps. The MCP-native sibling of Kestrel: an AI assistant reviews policies through tools on one Cloudflare Worker. Organisation: Personal. Year: 2026. Status: Live · private repo. Theme: AI-driven workflows. Stack: MCP, OAuth 2.1, Cloudflare Workers, D1, TypeScript.

chunks.title: Kestrel MCP · My role
chunks.text: Solo. The problem: Bring policy review into the assistant an adviser already uses, with the same validation as the full app and no model bill on the server.

chunks.title: Kestrel MCP · How it works
chunks.text: Upload: A policy document through an MCP tool. Map: A 35-field roster with confidence and citations. Flag: Gaps flagged for the adviser. Save: Server-side validation on every save.

chunks.title: Kestrel MCP · What I built
chunks.text: An MCP server on one Cloudflare Worker: D1 with Drizzle, R2, KV and a Durable Object for MCP sessions. The assistant maps fields with confidence and citations; the server validates every save. OAuth 2.1 for MCP with Google as the identity provider; Google sign-in with CSRF protection for the web UI. An append-only audit table enforced by database triggers. Ported from a Python FastAPI version to TypeScript; 19 test files; CI deploys and migrates.

chunks.title: Kestrel MCP · Key decisions
chunks.text: Ship the product as tools for an assistant, not a separate UI. Validation happens on the server for every save, whatever the assistant sends. Least privilege: the assistant has no confirm or delete tool. Users bring their own assistant, so the server spends almost nothing on inference.

chunks.title: Kestrel MCP · Results
chunks.text: 35 policy fields in the roster. ~19 MCP tools. 1 Cloudflare Worker.

chunks.title: TWC · Overview
chunks.text: TWC, an expense splitter with its own agent loop. A group expense splitter whose centrepiece is a receipt-reading agent. It runs entirely in the browser, on an agent loop I wrote from scratch. Drop in a receipt photo and an agent drafts the split for one-tap approval, entirely in the browser. Organisation: Personal. Year: 2025. Status: Live · Open source. Theme: AI-native products. Stack: Agent loop, Vision, React, TypeScript, Zod.

chunks.title: TWC · My role
chunks.text: Solo: design and build; open source. The problem: Splitting a group dinner from a receipt photo, in mixed currencies, is slow and error-prone.

chunks.title: TWC · How it works
chunks.text: Upload: A receipt photo, in the browser. Read: A vision model returns line items, validated by Zod. Plan: The agent drafts the split with idempotent tools. Approve: One tap to accept; nothing is written before.

chunks.title: TWC · What I built
chunks.text: An agent loop of up to 32 iterations with streamed phase labels and permission-gated tool dispatch. Receipt vision with structured outputs validated by Zod. A token-bucket rate limiter (10 a minute, 100 an hour), a preflight that rejects oversized images or context before spending tokens, and retries that honour Retry-After. A data-consent dialog per model provider; 43 test files; CI lints, tests, builds and deploys. One client interface over Anthropic, OpenAI and local OpenAI-compatible servers, each a hand-written fetch call. API keys stay in a passphrase-encrypted vault in the browser, with spend caps.

chunks.title: TWC · Key decisions
chunks.text: Plan mode removes write tools from the schema instead of trusting the prompt. Conversation pruning at 60% of the context budget. Money held in integer minor units so balances reconcile to zero.

chunks.title: TWC · Results
chunks.text: 32 max iterations per agent run. 0 servers or databases. 43 test files.

chunks.title: Leeseidon · Overview
chunks.text: Leeseidon, investment tracking with an encryption-blind server. A privacy-first investment tracker. Agents turn statements, PDFs and screenshots into trades, and the sync server only ever sees ciphertext. Agents read your statements; the sync server only ever stores ciphertext. Organisation: Personal. Year: 2026. Status: Live. Theme: AI-native products. Stack: React, TypeScript, Cloudflare Workers, AES-GCM, OAuth.

chunks.title: Leeseidon · My role
chunks.text: Solo: product, design and build. The problem: Portfolio trackers want your financial data on their servers. I wanted the analytics without handing that over.

chunks.title: Leeseidon · How it works
chunks.text: Drop: A CSV, PDF or screenshot. Extract: A multi-turn agent turns it into trades through schematized tools. Reconcile: The same engine as manual entry. Sync: Encrypted on the device; the server stores ciphertext.

chunks.title: Leeseidon · What I built
chunks.text: Multi-turn agents extract trades from CSV, PDF and images through schematized tools. A model-agnostic tool executor with streaming, retries and rate-limit handling. One isomorphic TypeScript core powers the web app and a CLI that ships Claude Code skills. A Monte Carlo retirement planner runs in a Web Worker. Auth: PBKDF2-SHA512 passwords, Google OAuth with single-use state, hashed session tokens, per-email lockout, and responses that never reveal whether an account exists. Index columns are HMAC-blinded, not just encrypted. Single sign-on across six apps on subdomains, with server-side revocation. A billing webhook (Polar) with HMAC signature checks and entitlements. Strict CSP, HSTS and COOP headers at the edge; a PKCE flow for the CLI. 757 test files; CI runs app, worker and CLI tests plus a data-contract check.

chunks.title: Leeseidon · Key decisions
chunks.text: The vault passphrase never leaves the device. AI-parsed statements go through the same engine as manual entry.

chunks.title: Leeseidon · Results
chunks.text: E2E encrypted sync. 1 TypeScript core for web and CLI. 6 apps on one sign-in. 757 test files.

chunks.title: Tide Tally · Overview
chunks.text: Tide Tally, an offline-first expense tracker with an agent. A mobile-first expense tracker. The home screen shows how much is left, and logging a spend takes three taps. It works offline, and an agent turns receipts and statements into draft expenses you review before anything is saved. Three taps to log a spend, even with no signal; hand the agent a receipt or statement and review what it drafts. Organisation: Personal. Year: 2026. Status: Live. Theme: AI-native products. Stack: React, TypeScript, IndexedDB, Cloudflare D1, WebGL, Capacitor, OAuth.

chunks.title: Tide Tally · My role
chunks.text: Solo: product, design and build, with Claude Code. The problem: Most budgeting apps open onto a dashboard, need a signal, and nag. Logging a $3.40 coffee should take seconds, in a basement food court or on the MRT.

chunks.title: Tide Tally · How it works
chunks.text: Capture: The numpad is the home screen: amount, category, save. Store: Every write lands on the device first (IndexedDB). Sync: A Cloudflare Pages Function and D1 sync in the background. Ask: The agent reads a receipt or statement and drafts expenses. Review: You confirm drafts; other software can log through OAuth.

chunks.title: Tide Tally · What I built
chunks.text: React 19, TypeScript and Tailwind on Vite, with a hand-written WebGL shader for the water. Offline-first storage in IndexedDB (Dexie) with background sync to a Cloudflare Pages Function and D1, on one origin. An agent that turns an uploaded receipt or statement into draft expenses on the same review screen as manual entry. An OAuth device flow with three scopes, so a coding agent or a script can log an expense, with an OpenAPI spec generated from the route table and a skill package published by CI. Android and iOS builds with Capacitor; Vitest, Playwright (including an offline-capture suite) and invariant checks in CI. An eval harness scores the receipt agent's per-field precision and recall against labelled receipts. A hard AI cost cap: the worst case is reserved in SQL before every call, then settled. A tenant-isolation suite drives the real router with two sessions; 308 test files. Sign in with Apple and Google, checked server-side; family sharing. Subscription billing built for Paddle, the App Store and Google Play, with signed notifications verified. Moved the agent from Chat Completions to the OpenAI Responses API.

chunks.title: Tide Tally · Key decisions
chunks.text: Uploaded documents are read once in the request and never stored. The agent only drafts; nothing reaches the ledger until you save it. Dropped end-to-end encryption that depended on a key another app could rotate, and said so plainly in the privacy note. A free stack by design: Cloudflare Pages, Functions and D1.

chunks.title: Tide Tally · Results
chunks.text: 3 taps to log an expense. Offline every write lands on the device first. Live at tally.leeseidon.com.

chunks.title: Verona · Overview
chunks.text: Verona, a wedding app an agent can drive. A mobile-first wedding app for guests and couples: RSVPs, seating and a live photo wall. Every feature is in an OpenAPI contract, so an agent can use the app too. RSVPs, seating and a live photo wall, with an API an agent can use. Organisation: Personal. Year: 2026. Status: Live. Theme: AI-native products. Stack: Next.js, Supabase, row-level security, PWA.

chunks.title: Verona · My role
chunks.text: Solo: product, design and build. The problem: Wedding planning is spread across spreadsheets, chat groups and paper seating plans.

chunks.title: Verona · How it works
chunks.text: Contract: One OpenAPI contract for the UI and the API. App: A Next.js PWA on Cloudflare Workers. Data: Supabase Postgres with row-level security and realtime. Agent: A bring-your-own agent can use every feature.

chunks.title: Verona · What I built
chunks.text: Next.js (App Router) PWA on Cloudflare Workers. Supabase Postgres with row-level security, Google sign-in and realtime updates. Photo uploads to object storage and a moderated live photo wall. Vitest in CI with auto-deploy; English, Chinese and Malay. CI checks the OpenAPI contract against the generated agent skills. Claude Code skills generated from the OpenAPI spec, and scoped tokens for agents. Row-level security keyed on each wedding, so couples never see each other's data. A realtime load test against the free tier's limit of about 200 connections. Web Push notifications, consent records and an admin view of usage and cost; 107 test files.

chunks.title: Verona · Key decisions
chunks.text: An OpenAPI parity contract so an agent can use every feature. Free-tier-only infrastructure as a cost guardrail.

chunks.title: Verona · Results
chunks.text: 3 languages. RLS row-level security in Postgres. Live at verona.leeseidon.com.

chunks.text: Résumé Builder, a Claude Code plugin. A Claude Code plugin that turns career notes into tailored, ATS-safe résumés and cover letters, with the deterministic build steps exposed as MCP tools. Three skills and an MCP server that turn career notes into tailored, ATS-safe résumés. Organisation: Personal. Year: 2026. Status: Private. Theme: Tooling for AI work. Stack: Claude Code plugin, MCP, LaTeX, Python.

chunks.title: Résumé Builder · My role
chunks.text: Built with one collaborator, who reworked the UI and structure. I directed Claude Code, which wrote most of my part. The problem: Every application meant rewriting a CV from a blank page, and claims drifted from what actually happened.

chunks.title: Résumé Builder · How it works
chunks.text: Notes: One source of truth for career facts. Tailor: A skill maps a job description to evidence. Build: MCP tools compile the PDF. Check: An ATS check for ATS templates.

chunks.title: Résumé Builder · What I built
chunks.text: Skills for building the career notes, tailoring a résumé and writing a cover letter. An MCP server that exposes the deterministic build steps (compile, checks) as tools. A local companion app alongside the plugin. PDF and .docx output; compiles time out safely and writes are atomic. CI runs pytest, a front-end build and manifest validation.

chunks.title: Résumé Builder · Key decisions
chunks.text: Every CV is generated from one source of truth. Deterministic steps are tools; judgement stays with the model and the person.

chunks.title: Résumé Builder · Results
chunks.text: 3 skills. 15 MCP tools. PDF + .docx output.

chunks.title: eval-code · Overview
chunks.text: eval-code, an agent-first eval workbench. A workbench for LLM, RAG and multi-agent projects: ingest and clean data, define an eval target, run evals under a hard spend cap and compare runs. A workspace for LLM, RAG and agent projects: data in, evals run under a hard spend cap, failures compared. Organisation: Personal. Year: 2026. Status: Early. Theme: Tooling for AI work. Stack: Python, LLM evals, RAG, Langfuse, DuckDB, Next.js.

chunks.title: eval-code · My role
chunks.text: Solo; early stage. The problem: LLM projects live in scattered notebooks, and eval runs can quietly burn money.

chunks.title: eval-code · How it works
chunks.text: Ingest: A raw dataset. Explore: Clean it and chart it. Evaluate: Run against a target under a hard spend cap. Compare: Compare runs and drill into failures.

chunks.title: eval-code · What I built
chunks.text: Dataset ingest, cleaning and chart-based exploration. Eval targets for RAG and agent systems. A spend tracker that stops runs at a cap; the CLI requires a maximum spend. LLM-as-judge adapters and RAG metrics: retrieval hit rate and citation precision. Langfuse tracing and permission modes (read-only, workspace write). Polars and DuckDB for data; FastAPI with server-sent events and a Next.js UI. 82 pytest files and 11 Playwright specs.

chunks.title: eval-code · Key decisions
chunks.text: Agent-first: the same tools serve the UI and an agent. Spend limits are enforced, not just reported.

chunks.title: eval-code · Results
chunks.text: Hard spend cap on every run. 82 pytest files. 11 Playwright specs.

chunks.title: Clinical NLP in production · Overview
chunks.text: Clinical NLP in production. A production NLP pipeline for a healthcare environment: entity extraction from clinical notes feeding a classifier that predicts clinical interventions, with explanations clinicians can read. Fine-tuned BioClinicalBERT and a downstream classifier, explained to clinicians. Organisation: AI Singapore. Year: 2024. Status: Employer. Theme: Applied ML and RAG. Stack: PyTorch, BioClinicalBERT, Kedro, MLflow, FastAPI.

chunks.title: Clinical NLP in production · My role
chunks.text: AI engineer on the project: data preparation, fine-tuning, evaluation and serving. Also mentored 12 apprentices across two cohorts. The problem: Clinical notes are unstructured, and clinicians need to see why a model made each call before they trust it.

chunks.title: Clinical NLP in production · How it works
chunks.text: Prepare: Clean and explore clinical notes. Extract: Fine-tuned BioClinicalBERT tags entities. Predict: A classifier predicts interventions. Explain: EBM shows clinicians why. Serve: FastAPI and Docker, tracked in MLflow.

chunks.title: Clinical NLP in production · What I built
chunks.text: Data cleaning and exploration of unstructured clinical notes. BioClinicalBERT fine-tuned in PyTorch for named-entity recognition, with other BERT models as baselines. Extracted entities feed a downstream intervention classifier. Evaluated on held-out data (precision, recall, F1); Kedro pipelines and MLflow tracking. Served with FastAPI and Docker, and handed over with documentation. RAG over clinical literature to disambiguate extracted entities. Worked with clinical domain experts, with patient-data privacy as a constraint throughout.

chunks.title: Clinical NLP in production · Key decisions
chunks.text: Explainable Boosting Machines so clinicians can read each prediction. Hyperparameter tuning with documented quality, latency and compute-cost trade-offs.

chunks.title: Clinical NLP in production · Results
chunks.text: NER feeding an intervention classifier. 12 apprentices mentored. EBM explanations for clinicians.

chunks.title: LedgerLens · Overview
chunks.text: LedgerLens, a fine-tuned model that reads bank statements. Phone photos of small-business bank statements and invoices go in. Checked transaction rows, a cash-flow analysis, cited red flags and a credit memo come out. A 4B vision model fine-tuned with LoRA reads statements better than an 8B model, at half the cost per page. Organisation: Personal. Year: 2026. Status: Experiment. Theme: Applied ML and RAG. Stack: LoRA, Qwen3-VL, Runpod, FastAPI, React.

chunks.title: LedgerLens · My role
chunks.text: Solo. I framed the question, designed the data, ran the training and checked the results. The problem: Can a small model, fine-tuned on synthetic documents, match a model twice its size on accuracy, speed and cost per page?

chunks.title: LedgerLens · How it works
chunks.text: Read: A page image goes to a serverless GPU endpoint and comes back as strict JSON. Check: Code checks every row against the printed running balance. Analyse: Code computes cash flow, balances and red flags, each citing its page and row. Write: The model writes the memo only from the computed figures.

chunks.title: LedgerLens · What I built
chunks.text: Qwen3-VL 4B fine-tuned with LoRA (Unsloth, one epoch, rank 16) on synthetic statements. Test sets built from statement layouts held back from training. Served on Runpod Serverless with structured output, validated with Pydantic. FastAPI and React app: upload, review table, analysis, memo.

chunks.title: LedgerLens · Key decisions
chunks.text: Score on layouts the model never saw, so the result is not memorisation. Report the weak result too: real phone photos of printed pages drop to 67%. Endpoints scale to zero when idle, so an unused demo costs nothing.

chunks.title: LedgerLens · Results
chunks.text: 96.5% of lines right on 1,499 unseen-layout pages, vs 57.8% for the 8B. 1.28 s per page vs 2.58 s, on the same GPU. $0.26 per 1,000 pages vs $0.52.

chunks.title: An agentic rebuild of a credit-memo pipeline · Overview
chunks.text: An agentic rebuild of a credit-memo pipeline. I had built a deterministic pipeline that turns financial statements into a credit memo. This rebuilds it with an orchestrator and specialist agents, on a different stack, so the two can be compared output for output. An orchestrator and parallel specialist agents redo a credit-memo pipeline I had built deterministically. Organisation: Personal. Year: 2026. Status: Experiment. Theme: Multi-agent systems. Stack: Claude, Amazon Bedrock, Python, Multi-agent, PyMuPDF.

chunks.title: An agentic rebuild of a credit-memo pipeline · My role
chunks.text: Solo: design and build. The problem: How does a design where agents plan their own steps compare with a fixed pipeline, on the same statements?

chunks.title: An agentic rebuild of a credit-memo pipeline · How it works
chunks.text: Spread: An orchestrator sends the PDF to three specialists: P&L, balance sheet, cash flow. Review: An analyst checks and edits the extracted table before anything else runs. Analyse: Three section specialists write the memo's financial section in parallel. Compare: Output keeps the old pipeline's format, so the two can be diffed.

chunks.title: An agentic rebuild of a credit-memo pipeline · What I built
chunks.text: Claude Sonnet 4.6 orchestrator and specialists, Haiku 4.5 for small tasks, on Amazon Bedrock. PyMuPDF and Azure Document Intelligence to read the PDF. Specialist tools: retrieve evidence, compute ratios, write a section draft. Specialists run concurrently; each section gets at most one retry. Handles statements in other languages, such as Korean.

chunks.title: An agentic rebuild of a credit-memo pipeline · Key decisions
chunks.text: A person confirms the extracted figures before the analysis runs. Same input and output format as the deterministic pipeline, so results compare directly. Retries with backoff on model timeouts, capped per section.

chunks.title: An agentic rebuild of a credit-memo pipeline · Results
chunks.text: 335 recorded runs. 3 specialists running in parallel per phase. 2 phases: extract, then analyse.

chunks.title: A WhatsApp seminar funnel for financial advisers · Overview
chunks.text: A WhatsApp seminar funnel for financial advisers. A team of financial advisers runs seminars. This takes each sign-up from registration to confirmation, Zoom link, seminar and 1-1 follow-up over WhatsApp, with their Google Sheet as the record. Runs a seminar funnel over WhatsApp from the client's own Google Sheet. I then advised the client to use a SaaS product instead. Organisation: Personal. Year: 2026. Status: Client project. Theme: AI-driven workflows. Stack: WhatsApp, MCP, Claude Cowork, Google Sheets, TypeScript.

chunks.title: A WhatsApp seminar funnel for financial advisers · My role
chunks.text: Solo: design and build for a client, and the recommendation to replace it. The problem: Seminar reminders had to go out on time and never twice, because double messages to strangers get a WhatsApp number banned.

chunks.title: A WhatsApp seminar funnel for financial advisers · How it works
chunks.text: Sync: Read sign-ups from the client's Google Sheet every hour. Plan: Code decides who is due for which message, not a prompt. Approve: Advisers check and approve in Claude Cowork over MCP. Send: One WhatsApp process sends, and handles STOP on arrival.

chunks.title: A WhatsApp seminar funnel for financial advisers · What I built
chunks.text: Hourly scheduler: sync, plan, consent check, render, reserve in a ledger. One always-on WhatsApp process is the only sender; the ledger is its queue. MCP tools so advisers read replies and approve messages in Claude Cowork. Landing page, admin console and a Google Apps Script backend for sign-ups.

chunks.title: A WhatsApp seminar funnel for financial advisers · Key decisions
chunks.text: Scheduling is a tested function with an injected clock, so it can't double-send. The system makes no model calls; the client's only AI cost is the Cowork seat they already had. Messages are timed from the seminar date, so late sign-ups still get the Zoom link before the seminar. Advised the client to move to a SaaS product: their team could run it, it removed the WhatsApp ban risk, it cost less at their volume and it had features they needed.

chunks.title: A WhatsApp seminar funnel for financial advisers · Results
chunks.text: Live landing page took real seminar sign-ups. 0 model calls made by the system itself. SaaS recommended over my own build.

chunks.title: Kaki Arcade · Overview
chunks.text: Kaki Arcade, party games on the TV with phones as controllers. A browser games platform for a room of people. The TV runs the game; each player's phone becomes the controller after a QR scan. It ships with three original games. One TV shows the game. Up to 8 players scan a QR code and their phones become controllers. Nothing to install. Organisation: Personal. Year: 2026. Status: In development (Nov 2026). Theme: Games and everyday apps. Stack: WebRTC, Cloudflare Durable Objects, PixiJS, TypeScript, Playwright.

chunks.title: Kaki Arcade · My role
chunks.text: Claude Code wrote all of the code. I set the requirements, acceptance criteria and stack, and did the testing. The problem: I wanted games friends and family could play together at home on the TV, without consoles, accounts or app installs.

chunks.title: Kaki Arcade · How it works
chunks.text: Host: The TV opens a room and shows a QR code. Join: Phones scan it; a small server only pairs the devices. Play: Phones send input straight to the TV, which runs the game. Fallback: A relay is used only if a direct link fails.

chunks.title: Kaki Arcade · What I built
chunks.text: TypeScript monorepo: one Vite web app for the TV and the phones. PixiJS (WebGL) renders the games on the TV. WebRTC data channels from each phone to the TV. Cloudflare Worker with one Durable Object per room for pairing; idle rooms cost nothing. Vitest for game rules; Playwright runs a TV plus several phones over real WebRTC.

chunks.title: Kaki Arcade · Key decisions
chunks.text: My call: phone input goes straight to the TV, not through a server, to cut lag and hosting cost. The TV is the only source of game state, with seeded, repeatable game logic. Tested at home with 6+ friends; the UI problems they hit were fixed in later builds.

chunks.title: Kaki Arcade · Results
chunks.text: 32 ms input delay (p95) with 8 phones, against a 50 ms target, on emulated phones. 8 players per room. 3 original games.

chunks.title: Equidistant · Overview
chunks.text: Equidistant, where a group should meet. Give it where each person is, and it names a place they can all reach within a time budget, with each person's travel time shown. Names a real place in Singapore that everyone in a group can reach fairly by travel time. Organisation: Personal. Year: 2026. Status: Live. Theme: Games and everyday apps. Stack: R5, Python, TypeScript, Static site.

chunks.title: Equidistant · My role
chunks.text: Solo. I made the product and design decisions. The problem: Groups meet wherever they went last time, which suits one person. Map distance is the wrong measure in a city with dense transit; travel time is what matters.

chunks.title: Equidistant · How it works
chunks.text: Pin: Each person drops a pin and picks how they travel. Load: The app fetches one small precomputed file per person. Combine: The browser works out when the last person would arrive. Name: It ranks real places and shows each person's time.

chunks.title: Equidistant · What I built
chunks.text: Travel times precomputed for all of Singapore with R5 (r5py), on a weekday departure window. Five modes: public transport, MRT and LRT only, bus only, cycling, driving. Static site with no backend; locations stay in the URL and in memory. About 30 KB fetched per pin.

chunks.title: Equidistant · Key decisions
chunks.text: Rank by travel time, not distance. Precompute everything, so no server ever sees anyone's location. Each person can use a different mode in the same search. When nothing fits the time budget, show the budget that would work.

chunks.title: Equidistant · Results
chunks.text: Live used by friends and family. 5 travel modes. 0 servers that see a location.

chunks.title: Jadeborne Kingdoms · Overview
chunks.text: Jadeborne Kingdoms, an online card game. A free, web-first card game of hidden roles and city building. Friends play online from an invite link, and bots fill empty seats. A card game of hidden roles and city building, set in the Three Kingdoms and Journey to the West. Play with friends or bots. Organisation: Personal. Year: 2026. Status: Live alpha. Theme: Games and everyday apps. Stack: Cloudflare Durable Objects, React, react-three-fiber, TypeScript.

chunks.title: Jadeborne Kingdoms · My role
chunks.text: I designed the rules and the architecture; Claude Code wrote the code. The problem: A hidden-role game breaks if any player's browser can see other players' cards.

chunks.title: Jadeborne Kingdoms · How it works
chunks.text: Invite: A link brings friends into a match. Deal: The server deals roles and cards. Play: Live turns over WebSockets. Fill: Bots take empty seats.

chunks.title: Jadeborne Kingdoms · What I built
chunks.text: React and Vite with a 2.5D table in react-three-fiber; installable as a PWA. Cloudflare Workers, with one Durable Object per match running the game. D1 for accounts and progress, R2 for assets and replays.

chunks.title: Jadeborne Kingdoms · Key decisions
chunks.text: The server runs the game, and hidden cards are never sent to a player who shouldn't see them. I wrote the rules spec and the optional additions on top of the classic mode. I set the bot difficulty targets.

chunks.title: Jadeborne Kingdoms · Results
chunks.text: 73.4% of 500 games won by the normal bot over the easy one (target 70%). 2.6 ms slowest bot move. Live alpha, played by friends and family.
